absent: Broadcast event dispatch and wakeup delivery behavior beyond setup and mask maintenance.
Periodic broadcast start, stop, enter, and exit transitions beyond what setup and offline show.
One-shot tick programming details, deadlines, and clocksource interactions.
Full clock_event_device and tick_device field layouts and numeric ABI values.
Error broadcast fallback behavior and missing-broadcast warning policy internals.
Module reference counting and device lifecycle ownership rules.
Sysfs attribute set beyond current-device display.

findings.text: Per-CPU tick device installation assigns the global timekeeping CPU on first setup, starts in periodic mode, preserves prior handler and deadline across replacement, pins non-local interrupt affinity, consults broadcast eligibility, then arms periodic or one-shot mode. Replacement preserves continuity by silencing the old handler before switching pointers.

Broadcast eligibility distinguishes placeholder devices from functional local devices. Placeholders are forced to periodic handling, given a broadcast callback, added to the broadcast population, and trigger periodic start or one-shot setup. Functional devices leave the broadcast population when power independent and when not flagged for broadcast, then in one-shot mode clear local one-shot state and let the caller proceed, while in periodic mode they may shut down an unused broadcaster and report whether the caller must stay shut down.

One-shot broadcast setup is idempotent. A repeated entry only clears local one-shot and pending membership and returns. First entry installs the one-shot broadcast handler, clears forced-event state, parks the deadline at maximum, and when transitioning from periodic merges the periodic population minus the local CPU into the one-shot population and pre-loads the next period into affected per-CPU deadlines. It skips reprogramming if already in one-shot state and otherwise arms only when the one-shot population is non-empty.

Arming the broadcaster always ensures one-shot state before programming the deadline and then migrates its interrupt affinity to the requesting CPU. Affinity migration is skipped unless the device advertises dynamic IRQ support and only when the target set differs from the current set.

Clearing one-shot membership removes a CPU from both the one-shot and pending broadcast sets. Full offline removal additionally clears the force set and drops any per-CPU one-shot wakeup association. Next-deadline initialization fans a single deadline out to every per-CPU event device named by the caller mask, skipping CPUs without an installed device.

Clock-change notification has global and local forms: one marks every possible CPU scheduler state for clock recheck, the other marks only the local CPU. One-shot capability is reported per CPU by comparing the local tick mode under IRQs disabled. No-operation variants exist for configurations without broadcast, one-shot, or clock notification support.

Replacement selection first checks CPU coverage, locality preference, and IRQ affinity movability, rejecting a non-local candidate when a local device already exists. It then prefers one-shot capable devices, refuses to install a periodic-only device while one-shot mode is active or over a one-shot current device, and otherwise prefers higher rating while favoring a local device over a differently scoped peer. Activation exchanges devices, reinstalls per-CPU state, and notifies one-shot support when the newcomer is one-shot capable.

Clock event replacement scans the global detached-device list, skips the outgoing device and attached devices, keeps the best candidate by the suitability predicate while holding module references, installs the winner on the local CPU, and unlinks the outgoing device. It reports success only when a successor was found.

Unbinding distinguishes unused, locally active, and remotely active devices. An unused device is unlinked immediately; the active device on the target CPU requests retry through replacement; any other attached device reports busy. The retry path runs on the target CPU under the clockevents lock, and the public wrapper serializes remote requests with a mutex.

Registration initializes every device to detached state, supplies a local CPU mask when absent, rewrites a global all-CPU mask to the possible set, links the device, probes for immediate use, and announces released devices. Combined configuration stores tick bounds, derives scaling and nanosecond bounds, then registers. The no-operation handler is an empty callback used to silence replaced or shut down devices.

Frequency configuration applies only to one-shot capable devices, derives a sleep horizon from tick capacity and frequency with a minimum of one second and a cap for very large ranges, then derives multiplier, shift, and minimum and maximum nanosecond deltas. Frequency update reprograms an armed one-shot deadline, re-enters periodic state for periodic devices, and does nothing for other states.

Frequency update first offers the device to the broadcast layer under IRQs disabled; only when the device is not the broadcaster does it use the direct path. The broadcast path succeeds only for the installed broadcast device and serializes reconfiguration with the broadcast lock.

Suspend walks registered devices in reverse and resume walks forward, each skipping detached devices and invoking only implemented callbacks. CPU offline first detaches broadcast state, shuts down the local tick device, purges released devices, and unlinks orphaned single-CPU non-broadcast devices expected to be detached. Broadcast offline clears periodic and enabled membership, clears one-shot state, and shuts down an unused periodic broadcaster.

Shared tick state is protected by three disciplines: a global jiffies lock guards the shared next period snapshot; the broadcast lock with IRQs saved or held guards broadcast mode, masks, broadcaster installation, and offline transitions; the clockevents lock with IRQs disabled or saved guards the device lists, registration, replacement, unbind retry, offline cleanup, and sysfs current-device reads, with a mutex serializing unbind requests and local IRQ save around frequency updates and mode queries.

Observed per-CPU tick state pairs an installed event-device pointer with a periodic or one-shot mode, plus a scheduler flag word used to request clock rechecks. Observed event-device state includes handler, deadlines, forced-event flag, features, rating, CPU set, IRQ number, broadcast callback, module owner, lifecycle callbacks, list linkage, and tick and nanosecond bounds. Observed broadcast state includes an installed device, a mode, and periodic, enabled, one-shot, pending, and force CPU sets.

Sysfs current-device reporting resolves a broadcast pseudo-device to global broadcast state and any other identifier to the corresponding per-CPU tick device, then emits the installed device name only when a device is present. Resolution differs by configuration: broadcast-aware builds check the broadcast pseudo-device first, while minimal builds always use per-CPU state.
The clockevents bus identity exposes a bus name and a per-device name prefix, with one per-CPU device instance backing the sysfs representation.

Broadcast mask updates have ordering hazards: merging periodic membership into one-shot state during replacement rather than periodic transition would leave stale bits that suppress later deadline updates, and failing to clear the newly one-shot local CPU would suppress its first broadcast entry. Frequency and deadline reads may observe a past value, which is tolerated because programming a past deadline forces an immediate event.
